question: What does God offer Solomon at Gibeon, what does Solomon ask for, and what does he receive beyond his request?
What portrait of Solomon's reign do the final verses present right after the request for wisdom, and what questions can they raise in light of Deuteronomy 17:16-17?
The word חָכְמָה (chokhmah, “wisdom”) is asked for together with “knowledge” to “go out and come in before this people”: what is this wisdom for, according to Solomon's request?
If God said to you “ask what you want,” what would you ask for, and what does that reveal about your priorities?
What does Solomon ask of Hiram, and what does he offer in return?
How does Solomon reconcile the greatness of the house he will build with the statement that “the highest heavens” cannot contain God?
The word חָכָם (chakham, “wise, skilled”) is used for the craftsman sent by Hiram: what does this word suggest about the relationship between wisdom and manual work in the Bible?
The work of the temple also used the forced labor of foreigners: how do you react to this less glorious side of a grand religious work?
Where does Solomon build the house of the LORD, and what earlier episodes does the text link to this place?
What meaning do the cherubim carved and embroidered in the Most Holy Place and on the veil have?
The word כְּרוּב (kerub, “cherub”) appears on the walls, in the Most Holy Place and on the veil: in what other biblical texts do cherubim appear, and with what function?
The pillars receive names, Jachin and Boaz: what words would you like to be “at the entrance” of your house or of your life?
How is the “cast metal sea” described, and what was it for?
Why does the text list in such detail the gold and bronze utensils of the temple?
The great basin is called יָם (yam, “sea”): what could this word evoke for an Israelite, in light of Genesis 1 and the Psalms?
The basins were for washing, and the priests washed in the sea before serving: what preparation do you make before drawing near to God?
Who brings the ark to the temple, and what was inside it?
At what exact moment does the cloud fill the house, and what link does the text make between united praise and God's presence?
The word עָנָן (anan, “cloud”) recalls the cloud of the exodus and of the tabernacle: what does it mean when it fills the temple so that the priests cannot minister?
Singers and musicians sounded “as one”: what does the unity of a community have to do with the worship it offers?
What situations does Solomon present to God in his prayer, one after another?
How does Solomon answer his own question “will God really dwell with man on the earth?”, and what idea of the temple does this prayer express?
The verb סָלַח (salach, “forgive”) is the most repeated request in the prayer: in what kinds of situations does Solomon hope God will forgive?
Solomon also prays for the foreigner who comes from afar: who are the “outsiders” you would include in your prayers?
What happens right after Solomon's prayer, and how do the people react?
What warning does God give about the temple itself, and how would it be read by those who returned from exile, after the Babylonians destroyed the temple?
The verb כָּנַע (kana, “humble oneself”) opens the list of attitudes in 7:14: what else does the verse ask of the people, and what does God promise to do?
The verse speaks of healing the land: what would need to be healed in the place where you live, and where would you begin?
What cities does Solomon build or rebuild, and for what purpose?
Why does Solomon move Pharaoh's daughter elsewhere, and what does this say about his concern for holiness?
The word מִצְוָה (mitsvah, “commandment”) appears linked to Moses, to David and to the king: what sources of order does the chapter bring together for the temple worship?
Worship followed a calendar of Sabbaths, New Moons and feasts: what regular rhythm helps you live your faith?
What does the queen of Sheba come to do, what does she see, and how does she react?
According to the queen of Sheba, why did God put Solomon on the throne, and what does this have to do with God's love for Israel?

The queen says Solomon was made king “to carry out justice and righteousness,” with the word צְדָקָה (tsedaqah, “righteousness”): how does this compare with the description of riches that dominates the chapter?
The queen says “not even half was told to me”: in what area of your life did you only believe after seeing with your own eyes?
What advice do the elders give Rehoboam, what advice do the young men give, and which does he follow?
How does the text bring together Rehoboam's responsibility and the fulfillment of God's word through Ahijah in the division of the kingdom?
The word עֹל (ol, “yoke”) is repeated in the people's request and in the king's answer: what does this image say about how the people felt Solomon's rule?
The elders say that if the king speaks kind words, the people will serve him: how does your way of speaking affect those who depend on you?
What does Rehoboam plan to do against the northern tribes, and why does he give up?
What groups leave Jeroboam's kingdom and go to Judah, and why does the Chronicler make a point of recording this?
The verb לָחַם (lacham, “fight”) appears in Rehoboam's plan and in God's prohibition: why does the prophet call those the king wanted to fight “brothers”?
The people “listened to the word of the LORD” and gave up fighting their brothers: what conflict should you stop waging?
What happens to Rehoboam when his kingdom is established, and what consequence comes in the fifth year?
What does the replacement of Solomon's gold shields with bronze shields symbolize about Rehoboam's kingdom?
The verb עָזַב (azav, “leave, forsake”) appears in the king's failure and in God's answer: what correspondence does Shemaiah's message establish?
God says the people will learn the difference between serving Him and serving the kingdoms of the nations: what “masters” have you tried serving, and with what result?
What arguments does Abijah use against Jeroboam in his speech on Mount Zemaraim?
How does the text explain the victory of Judah, surrounded by the ambush, against an army twice its size?
Abijah speaks of a “covenant of salt,” with the word מֶלַח (melach, “salt”): what could salt represent in a covenant, in light of Leviticus 2:13 and Numbers 18:19?
Judah prevailed “because they relied on the LORD”: what do you usually rely on when you feel at a disadvantage?
What reforms does Asa make at the beginning of his reign, and what happens to the land in this period?
How does Asa's prayer before Zerah describe God, and what does it say about human strength?
The verb שָׁעַן (shaan, “rely on”) appears in Asa's prayer: on whom does he say he relies, and why is it worth remembering this word when reading chapter 16?
Asa uses the time of peace to fortify the cities: what can you build now, in quiet times, for the hard days?
What is the message of Azariah son of Oded to Asa, and what period of Israel's history does he recall?
How should we understand that the covenant included death for whoever would not seek the LORD, and how should this clause be read today?
The verb מָצָא (matsa, “find, be found”) appears in the promise and in its fulfillment: under what conditions does the text say God is found?
Asa removes his own grandmother from her position because of an idol: what family loyalties can come into conflict with faithfulness to God?
How does Asa resolve the threat from Baasha, and where does he get the resources to do so?
What does Hanani mean by “the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth,” and why does he call Asa's action foolish?
The same verb שָׁעַן (shaan, “rely on”) of chapter 14 returns in Hanani's rebuke: on whom did Asa rely before, and on whom does he rely now?
Asa reacts with rage to correction and, in his illness, does not seek the LORD: how do you react when someone points out a mistake of yours?
Whom does Jehoshaphat send through the cities of Judah, and with what book do they teach?
What does the text say about Jehoshaphat's heart, and what relationship does it draw between his faithfulness and the stability of the kingdom?
The verb לָמַד (lamad, “teach”) describes the mission of the officials, Levites and priests: why would instructing the people be a reform as important as removing the high places?
The envoys “went throughout all the cities” teaching: how does the Word reach the people around you?
How many prophets does Ahab consult, what do they say, and why does Jehoshaphat still ask for another prophet?
How should we read Micaiah's vision of the “lying spirit,” and what does it say about God's judgment on Ahab?
The word רוּחַ (ruach, “spirit, wind”) appears in the vision and in Zedekiah's taunt: what question about true prophecy does the chapter raise?
The messenger asks Micaiah to speak like the others, and he refuses: in what situation do you feel pressure to say only what pleases?
How does Jehoshaphat organize justice in the cities and in Jerusalem, and what instructions does he give the judges?
Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for the alliance with Ahab but recognizes “some good” in him: how does the text balance criticism and recognition?
The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “judgment, justice”) is at the center of the instructions: what does it mean for the judges to judge “for the LORD”?
“With the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery”: where are you called to decide without favoritism?
Facing the threat from Moab and Ammon, what does Jehoshaphat do, and who gathers with him?
What role does praise have in the battle of this chapter, and what does the text suggest by putting the singers in front?
The verb אָמַן (aman, “believe, be firm”) appears in a play on words: “believe” and “you will be established”; what relationship does Jehoshaphat draw between faith and firmness?
“We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You”: in what situation do you need to pray this prayer?
What does Jehoram do as soon as he is established on the throne, and what family influence does the text point to?
Why does the letter of the prophet Elijah compare Jehoram with Jehoshaphat and Asa, and what does it announce?
God does not destroy the house of David because of the promise to give him a נִיר (nir, “lamp”): what does this image mean for the continuity of the dynasty?
Jehoram “departed to no one's regret”: what would you like people to remember about you?
Who counsels Ahaziah, and what is the result of this counsel?
What would have been at stake if Joash had died, in light of the promise made to David?
The verb חָבָא (chava, “hide”) appears for Ahaziah, who hides and is found, and for Joash, hidden in the temple: what contrast is there between the two hiding places?
Jehoshabeath risks her life to hide a child: who needs your courageous protection today?
How does Jehoiada prepare and carry out the coronation of Joash?
What relationship does the text establish between the covenant made by Jehoiada and the destruction of the temple of Baal?
The word בְּרִית (berit, “covenant”) appears three times: with whom is each covenant made, and what do they have in common?
Jehoiada protects the sanctuary even in the middle of a revolt: what limits do you keep even when you act with urgency?
How does Joash organize the collection to restore the temple, and how do the people respond?
What changes in Joash's life after Jehoiada's death, and what dependence does this reveal?
The text says Joash “did not remember,” with the verb זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”), the kindness of Jehoiada: what role does the memory of kindness received have in faithfulness?
Joash was faithful “all the days of Jehoiada”: does your faith depend on someone, and what would happen if that person were gone?
What army does Amaziah hire, and why does the man of God tell him to dismiss it?
Why is it strange that Amaziah worships the gods of Edom right after defeating them, and how does he react to the prophet?
The text says Amaziah did what was right, but “not wholeheartedly,” with the word שָׁלֵם (shalem, “whole, complete”): how does the rest of the chapter show this division?
Amaziah worries about the hundred talents lost, and the prophet answers “the LORD is able to give you much more”: what loss do you fear in obeying?
What achievements does the text attribute to Uzziah, and when did he prosper?
Why was entering the temple to burn incense such a grave offense, and what does Uzziah's punishment communicate?
The verb גָּבַהּ (gavah, “be high, be exalted”) describes Uzziah's heart “when he became powerful”: what relationship does the text draw between success and pride?
Uzziah “loved the soil”: what ordinary interests and talents can you live out as part of your service to God?
In what does Jotham follow his father, in what is he different, and what does the text say about the people?
What contrast is there between the king's faithfulness and the corruption that continues among the people?
Jotham grew powerful because he “ordered his ways,” with the verb כּוּן (kun, “establish, prepare”): what does it mean to order one's ways before God?
A short chapter can describe a stable life: what value do you give to quiet faithfulness, without great deeds?
What religious practices of Ahaz does the text list, and what defeats does he suffer?
Why do the prophet Oded and some leaders of Ephraim order the captives to be returned, and what echo does this scene have in Luke 10:30-37?
The word שִׁבְיָה (shivyah, “captives”) appears in Oded's speech and in the final scene: how are the captives treated when they are again seen as brothers?
In his distress, Ahaz “became even more unfaithful” and sought other gods: where do you run when you are hard-pressed?
What does Hezekiah do in the first month of his reign, and how long does the purification of the temple take?
How does Hezekiah explain Judah's misfortunes, and what solution does he propose?
The verb קָדַשׁ (qadash, “sanctify, consecrate”) is repeated for people, house and utensils: what does it mean to sanctify something, according to this chapter?
The text says the thing was done “suddenly,” and everyone rejoiced: is there something you have been putting off that you could begin now?
To whom does Hezekiah send letters inviting them to the Passover, and how are the letters received in Ephraim, Manasseh and Zebulun?
Why does Hezekiah pray for those who ate the Passover without being purified, and what does God's answer reveal about what matters most in worship?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return, turn back”) is repeated in Hezekiah's letter: who must return, to whom, and what will God do in response?
Many laughed at the messengers, but some humbled themselves and came: how do you react when an invitation of yours is met with mockery?
What do the people bring after the Passover, and what does the high priest tell Hezekiah about these heaps of offerings?
How does the text sum up Hezekiah's reign, and what relationship does it draw between seeking God “with all his heart” and prospering?
The word אֱמוּנָה (emunah, “faithfulness”) describes how the offerings were kept and distributed: why is faithfulness in administration highlighted here?
“We have eaten and been satisfied, and there is plenty left over”: how could you share what is left over in your life?
What practical measures does Hezekiah take in the face of Sennacherib, and what does he tell the people to encourage them?
What happens to Hezekiah after his healing, and how does the text describe his fall and his return?

The verb נָצַל (natsal, “deliver”) dominates the Assyrians' propaganda: what comparison does Sennacherib make between the God of Israel and the gods of the other nations, and how does the chapter answer?
God leaves Hezekiah “to test him, to know all that was in his heart”: what recent situation revealed something in your heart you did not know?
What practices of Manasseh does the text list, and what does he do in the very house of the LORD?
How does Manasseh change after being taken in chains to Babylon, and why does the Chronicler tell this story that 2 Kings does not have?
The verb עָתַר (atar, “entreat, be moved by entreaty”) describes Manasseh's prayer: what does God's answering this king say about the reach of forgiveness?
Amon imitated his father's sin, but not his humbling: what have you inherited from the people who formed you, and what do you need to choose not to inherit?
At what age does Josiah begin to seek God and to purify the country, and how far does this reform go?
What answer does the prophetess Huldah give the king, and why does his reaction on hearing the book change what will happen in his days?
The word סֵפֶר (sefer, “book”) appears many times after the book of the law is found: what path does the book travel, from the temple to the assembly of the people?
Josiah tears his clothes on hearing the words of the law: when was the last time a biblical text touched you so much that it changed something?
How does Josiah organize the Passover, and what role do the Levites have in serving others?
Why does Josiah not listen to the words of Neco, which the text says came “from the mouth of God,” and what does this suggest about discerning God's voice?
The word פֶּסַח (pesach, “Passover”) is repeated throughout the celebration: what did this feast recall, and why does the text say there had been none like it since Samuel?
All Judah mourns Josiah, and Jeremiah composes laments: how does your community deal with the loss of someone who did much good?
How many kings rule Judah after Josiah, and what happens to each one?
How does the text describe God's patience before the exile, and what does it mean to say “there was no remedy”?
The exile is explained as the time when the land “enjoyed its Sabbath rests,” with the word שַׁבָּת (shabbat, “Sabbath, rest”): what law of Leviticus 25-26 lies behind this idea?
The book ends with Cyrus's decree and the words “let him go up”: what does it mean to you that the story does not end in ruin?
